There's been massive overhaul of this pattern, see edit below. code is here: http://pastebin.com/r0SaN04T

I consider visitor pattern as the most complicated pattern. It took me a long time to figure it out but I think I got it and I would like to share it with v/learnprogramming.

For complete working example see http://pastebin.com/bCgB9Hka

The problem - I have a list of objects of different types based on a sub-type (base class). I want to do specific things to those objects based on their type. We can solve this using the visitor pattern.

edit: not sure why numbering is screwd, wierd.

  1. Create blank ConsoleApplication.
namespace ConsoleApplication2
{
 class Program
 {
 static void Main(string[] args)
 {
 }
 }
}
  1. Define the interfaces for making the visitor pattern possible.
 class Program
 {
 static void Main(string[] args)
 {
 }
 }

 interface IVisitor
 {
 void Visit(IElement element);
 }

 interface IElement
 {
 void Accept(IVisitor visitor);
 }
  1. Create a base class that inherits from IElement and implement it as below.
 abstract class Creature : IElement
 {
 public string Name { get; set; }

 public void Accept(IVisitor visitor)
 {
 visitor.Visit(this);
 }
 }
  1. Create derived objects from our Creature class, you can add more properties if you'd like, I'm keeping it simple for simplicity sake.
 class Person : Creature
 {

 }

 class Animal : Creature
 {

 }
  1. Create the visitor objects that describe what will be done to the specific types, inherit from IVisitor interface and implement it. I'm checking to see if the element is of specific type (is), if it is - I will cast it (as) and run my custom logic for that type.
 class PersonVisitor : IVisitor
 {
 public void Visit(IElement element)
 {
 if (element is Person)
 {
 Creature creature = element as Person;

 Console.WriteLine("{0} is a good {1}", creature.Name, "Person");
 }
 }
 }

 class AnimalVisitor : IVisitor
 {
 public void Visit(IElement element)
 {
 if (element is Animal)
 {
 Creature creature = element as Animal;

 Console.WriteLine("{0} is a good {1}", creature.Name, "Animal");
 }
 }
 }
  1. Now create a class that will be responsible for processing of collection of types that inherit from Creature base class. This class takes into its constructor collection of creatures and collection of visitors. It has Process() method responsible for iterating over all the visitors and executing each visitor against collection of creatures.
 class CreatureProcessor
 {
 private readonly List<IVisitor> visitors;
 private readonly List<Creature> creatures; 

 public CreatureProcessor(List<Creature> creatures, List<IVisitor> visitors)
 {
 this.creatures = creatures;
 this.visitors = visitors;
 }

 public void Process()
 {
 foreach (IVisitor visitor in visitors)
 {
 foreach (Creature creature in creatures)
 {
 creature.Accept(visitor);
 }
 }
 }
 }
  1. Write the Main() method code to see it in action. Create a collection of visitors. Create collection of creatures putting inside it different types of creatures. Create CreatureProcessor class passing into constructor list of creatures and visitors. Finally call CreatureProcessor.Process() method to see the results.
 static void Main(string[] args)
 {
 List<IVisitor> visitors = new List<IVisitor>();
 visitors.AddRange(new List<IVisitor>()
 {
 new PersonVisitor(),
 new AnimalVisitor()
 });

 List<Creature> creatures = new List<Creature>();
 creatures.AddRange(new List<Creature>()
 {
 new Person() { Name = "Frank" },
 new Person() { Name = "Tony" },
 new Person() { Name = "Amy" },
 new Animal() { Name = "Bubbles" },
 new Animal() { Name = "Max" }
 });

 CreatureProcessor creatureProcessor = new CreatureProcessor(creatures, visitors);
 creatureProcessor.Process();

 Console.ReadKey();
 }

Edit:

So the usage of IS and AS keywords is bad I was told.

  1. The IVisitor interface is now changed to define methods for each concrete type being visited.
 interface IVisitor
 {
 void VisitAnimal(Animal element);
 void VisitPerson(Person element);
 }
  1. PersonVisitor and AnimalVisitor have been replaced with single class CreatureVisitor that implements IVisitor and defines it.
 class CreatureVisitor : IVisitor
 {
 public void VisitAnimal(Animal element)
 {
 Console.WriteLine("{0} is a good Animal", element.Name);
 }

 public void VisitPerson(Person element)
 {
 Console.WriteLine("{0} is a good Person", element.Name);
 }
 }
  1. Creature base class Accept() method has been converted to abstract method, passing on the implementation to individual concrete types of Creature.
 class Person : Creature
 {
 public override void Accept(IVisitor visitor)
 {
 visitor.VisitPerson(this);
 }
 }

 class Animal : Creature
 {
 public override void Accept(IVisitor visitor)
 {
 visitor.VisitAnimal(this);
 }
 }

 abstract class Creature : IElement
 {
 public string Name { get; set; }

 public abstract void Accept(IVisitor visitor);
 }
  1. CreatureProcessor had list of visitors removed and replaced with single instance of CreatureVisitor that defines the per type implementation. As result there is no longer need for iterating over visitors, so now we only have single foreach loop.
 class CreatureProcessor
 {
 private readonly CreatureVisitor visitor;
 private readonly List<Creature> creatures;

 public CreatureProcessor(List<Creature> creatures, CreatureVisitor visitor)
 {
 this.creatures = creatures;
 this.visitor = visitor;
 }

 public void Process()
 {
 foreach (Creature creature in creatures)
 {
 creature.Accept(visitor);
 }
 }
 }
  1. Main method now only creates instance of CreatureVisitor and passes it to CreatureProcessor.
 static void Main(string[] args)
 {
 CreatureVisitor creatureVisitor = new CreatureVisitor();

 List<Creature> creatures = new List<Creature>();
 creatures.AddRange(new List<Creature>()
 {
 new Person() { Name = "Frank" },
 new Person() { Name = "Tony" },
 new Person() { Name = "Amy" },
 new Animal() { Name = "Bubbles" },
 new Animal() { Name = "Max" }
 });

 CreatureProcessor creatureProcessor = new CreatureProcessor(creatures, creatureVisitor);
 creatureProcessor.Process();

 Console.ReadKey();
 }

Programming Hate Into AI Will Be Controversial, But Possibly Necessary

Emotions are just a heuristic by which an organism chooses which set of behaviours and responses to apply in any given situation. Any AI that deals with a dangerous, changing and unpredictable environment is probably going to have some equivalent of emotions.

Imagine a probe on an alien planet. It examines its local environment, and when it's found out everything it can, it moves to a new place. While moving, it encounters a cliff. Knowing that the top of a cliff is a dangerous place, it carefully steers clear of the cliff.

If you were designing the software for such a probe you would probably use a state machine. It starts in MODE_EXAMINE, and then when it's finished examining everything around it, it goes into MODE_EXPLORE until it gets to a new place. As it approaches the cliff, it recognizes danger and goes back to MODE_AVOID, steering away from the cliff until it is safe again.

In this case the modes are functionally identical to emotional states. It starts out being curious, and then when it runs out of things to examine, it gets bored, which makes it want to seek out new things. As it gets close to the cliff, it gets scared, so it steers away from the cliff.
"Emotions are just a heuristic" - Never thought of it like that, well said. Just simple rules of thumb to help the organism handle different environments.

Mainstream AI articles are getting more and more ridiculous. Emotions will, if anything, be emergent (or unintended) behavior. The increasing complexity of AI systems resulting in behavior so complex as to seem nondeterministic is actually a huge downside of AI. The reason we're embracing it is because it just does such a better job at so many tasks than we can manually code. The best way to think of AI is thinking about how you might teach a computer to visually recognize a letter. You could teach it a million rules, but in the end as a human you're rarely if ever going to be able to catch every single possible way that letter could be written or formed, let alone improper formations (such as bad handwriting) that the AI ought expected to be able to recognize.

So what we do instead of manual coding is create a lot of little indicators about an image and then run the AI through thousands, millions, even more samples of that letter and let the AI train itself on exactly what tends to happen when it sees a given letter. And now the really cool thing is you can use that exact same system to now let the AI teach itself how to recognize a different letter, or even a letter in an entirely different alphabet. If the system is broad enough the training used to recognize a letter could even be the same training used to recognize, for instance, a dog.

Where do emotions come into play here? They don't. But in the end some of its behaviors may end up looking emotional. For instance imagine the training for the letter O was particularly broad and it has a tendency of thinking stuff like Ds and Qs are Os. It doesn't mean it likes Os and I don't think many people would believe that was the reason either. But as the complexity of the topics being learned by the AI and exactly how an output is formulated becomes increasingly incomprehensible, then we might indeed start labeling such behavior as emotions. So no we're not going to be programming hate or any emotion into anything. Just more pointless clickbait like seemingly 99% of the news nowadays.
